page: Microsoft Azure E2s_v6 is an x86_64 memory-optimized virtual machine belonging to the Esv6 family, running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features 2 dedicated vCPUs derived from a single physical Intel Xeon 8573C core with 2 threads per core, operating at a clock speed of 4.2 GHz. The processor includes a 260 MB L3 cache and supports advanced instruction sets such as AVX-512 and Intel AMX (Advanced Matrix Extensions). The instance is equipped with 16.0 GB of system memory, yielding a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core. It does not include local storage or onboard GPUs, but it is Premium Storage capable for remote disk attachments.

Benchmark data reveals a clear performance profile. Single-core performance is relatively competitive, with Geekbench single-core scores rating as strong (2149.0) and stress-ng single-core performance landing in the average tier. However, multi-core and memory bandwidth metrics show significant constraints. The multi-core stress-ng performance is rated as poor, and Geekbench multi-core scores are weak, reflecting the physical limitation of its single-core, dual-thread allocation. Memory bandwidth is also restricted, with large-block read and write speeds falling into the poor category at 21.51 GB/sec and 14.04 GB/sec respectively.

Given its hardware profile, the E2s_v6 offers qualitative cost efficiency for workloads that require a larger memory footprint relative to compute power but do not demand high multi-threaded performance. It is suited for lightweight database operations, basic caching layers, single-threaded data processing, and small-scale web serving. It is less suitable for heavy multi-threaded compilation, complex ray tracing, or intensive memory-bandwidth-bound tasks.
description: Microsoft Azure E2s_v6 is a memory-optimized virtual machine from the Esv6 family, powered by an Intel Xeon 8573C processor running on Microsoft Hyper-V. It features 2 dedicated vCPUs (1 physical core, 2 threads) clocked at 4.2 GHz, 16.0 GB of RAM, and no local storage. While single-core performance is strong in Geekbench tests, its multi-core capabilities and memory bandwidth are relatively weak due to the single physical core constraint. This instance is best suited for memory-intensive, single-threaded workloads, lightweight caching, and small databases.
